title: Leg two: cheaper money, and feeling richer

cues.text: Leg one moved the prices of things in financial markets. Leg two has to turn that into somebody actually spending money. And it does it in two ways.
The rates households and firms borrow at are tied to safe government rates at the same length of time.
So if the whole set of government rates comes down, those rates should come down too.
And if banks benefit from higher asset prices in the same way ordinary companies do, then their own cost of borrowing falls as well.
And a bank that funds itself more cheaply can lower the price of the loans it makes.

And that gives the sentence the whole policy rests on. Their words: this fall in the cost of capital should boost consumption and investment, by increasing incentives to borrow and reducing incentives to save.
One. The banking sector was badly damaged at exactly the time the policy was used. So anything travelling through it may be impaired.
Two. Households and smaller companies cannot borrow by selling bonds to investors in the first place. So they may not benefit from that route at all.
Three. And a bank that is short of capital of its own may simply keep the saving rather than pass it on.
And be fair to them, because they do not leave it there. They name three further routes by which small firms might still benefit.
Supply-chain effects. A small firm tied to a large one benefits either through extra demand, or through being paid more easily.
A cheaper pound makes a small exporter more competitive.
And falls in safe rates and in bank funding costs may be passed on to all borrowers anyway.
An obvious implication of a fall in gilt yields is that the government's own cost of borrowing is now lower. Gilts are exactly what was bought.
And their answer is that it will not change what the government does. Governments take a longer-term view. Their spending plans should therefore be unaffected by cyclical movements in interest rates.
When asset prices go up, the people who own those assets are richer. And higher wealth should mean more spending.
They put a number on it. Three hundred and seventy-five billion pounds of announced purchases will eventually boost British households' net financial wealth by about thirty per cent.
And they are open about who gets them. Those gains go largely to whoever holds the most financial assets. In particular, older and more affluent households.
For most pensions the two effects roughly cancel. The rate you can buy an income at falls with gilt yields — but the pot itself is worth more, for exactly the same reason.
But a scheme that was already short of money is likely to have been made worse off. Its assets and its promises both rose in value, which widened the gap between them.
As with all monetary policy, they say, there are winners and losers.
